extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; aspiring essayists, conversationalists, and observers of manners (early-18th-century literati)
extracted.subtask_short: writing genteel essays and character sketches
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for composing moral/observational essays and character sketches that convey virtue, cheerfulness, and agreeable company through anecdote, tone, and naturalness. Emphasises authenticity, modesty, sensory detail, and appropriate conduct in conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candour about oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural consequence of candour when we speak of ourselves: acknowledge faults rather than defending them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owning up to faults is not a degradation of greatness; perfection is not the attribute of man. Examples: a criminal who confesses gains pity and spares further shame; people who persist in wrong out of a mistaken notion of 'high spirit' are acting from little minds. Anti-pattern: obstinacy in the wrong, defending faults in servants, or refusing to acknowledge being on the faulty side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity / only claim what you perform
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing but what a man really performs that can be an honour to him; taking more credit in the world harms the conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to avoid boasting or claiming undue credit—false glory causes inward mortification. Implicit for writers: be honest about authorship and deeds (e.g., publisher vs. true author).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of style (elegant, argumentative, sublime)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator employs multiple styles—elegant, argumentative, and sublime—with equal success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the range of prose styles suited to subject and effect rather than sticking to a single mode; blending registers can be effective. Example: the paper switches between elegant description, argumentative moralising, and elevated (sublime) passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character by specific actions and small incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is best shown through concrete, habitual actions (what a person does), not abstract description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sir Roger salutes passers-by, insists on hiring watermen wounded in service (wooden leg), reacts to a masque—these small behaviors build a vivid portrait. Anti-pattern: long general statements about a person's qualities without illustrative anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use idiosyncratic prejudices and local detail to characterise
rubrics_metrics.description: Honest, even comic prejudices and local opinions (e.g., national pride, views about churches, London Bridge) can mark character vividly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sir Roger's proud prejudices about the navy, the Thames, and churches serve to reveal his temperament and social outlook. Employ culturally rooted remarks to lend authenticity; beware of caricature if overdone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness over affected versatility
rubrics_metrics.description: Varying one's behaviour to suit all humours is agreeable only when it springs from natural temper; pretending to be all things by artifice is degrading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt manners merely to win praise—such artful parts are 'prostitution' and unbecoming. Authentic flexibility (coming from one's temperament) is valuable; forced adaptation is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be agreeable by receiving rather than dictating
rubrics_metrics.description: The true art of being agreeable in company is to appear well-pleased with those you are with and to seem entertained rather than to bring entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receive law from the company, do not give it; avoid domineering, preaching, or making others the butt of derision. Anti-patterns: interrupting with one's own life-history, acting as a 'messenger' who derails the group's conversation, deriding the absent or embarrassing present company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wounding wit; favour friendly modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit that hurts or exposes individuals makes a person an unpleasant companion; humility and friendliness are more pleasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sharp sallies that 'pinch or tickle' making others uneasy are to be avoided. The agreeable companion contributes by disposition, good sense, good nature, and discretion rather than by ostentatious wit that harms others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules prevent poor work but do not make geniuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Precepts and rules may prevent bad practice (e.g., in poetry or conversation) but cannot by themselves produce great talent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges limits of formal precepts: they can check ineptitude but cannot substitute for natural genius or authentic taste. Implication for writers: learn rules but don't expect them to create exceptional art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in reproach and criticism among friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Letting a friend see his faults is delicate; reproaches should be strictly just and not too frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When giving correction, ensure it is for the friend's advantage, not to please oneself; excessive or unfair censure will alienate and diminish esteem. This serves as guidance for critique—be sparing and fair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory and natural imagery to foster mood (cheerfulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural scenery, sounds, colours, and the sun are effective in chearing the mind and promoting cheerfulness of tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: descriptions of Spring-Garden, choirs of birds, the sun as 'the great Soul of the Universe', and green as a restful colour that comforts the eye. Employ sensory, landscape, and colour imagery to induce the intended emotional atmosphere in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hide design beneath beauty: let usefulness be pleasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature (and good composition) conceals principal design beneath beauty—important parts are lodged in attractive forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: seeds are lodged in flowers—beauty masks function. For writers: make the craft (argument, moral, instruction) attractive, so the reader enjoys the form while the purpose is carried out; avoid didactic plainness that repels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't merely tell (illustrate moral points with narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and behavioural lessons are more persuasive when exemplified by anecdotes and particulars rather than abstract moralising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay uses stories (criminal at the bar; Sir Roger in Spring-Garden) to demonstrate points about candour, modesty, and cheerfulness. Anti-pattern: lecturing in generalities without illustrative cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use explanatory notes/footnotes for obscure references
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify historical or obscure allusions with brief explanatory notes so readers understand the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text supplies a footnote explaining La Hogue / Bantry Bay and other historical matters—useful editorial practice for making essays accessible to readers unfamiliar with particular events.
